- When sentiment is consistently bullish (≥0.67) and model forecasts are flat or rising slowly, expect overshoot or overconfidence in early price spikes; adjust downward by 5–10% for the next 5–7 days.
- If supply net is negative and bearish sentiment dominates (≥0.50), model forecasts tend to underestimate downside risk; add 3–5% buffer to forecast lows.
- After a sharp price spike (e.g., >10% from prior day), model often overreacts and continues upward; cap forecast slope at 1–2% per day for 3–5 days.
- When official events are frequent and supply net is negative, model tends to lag in recognizing downward pressure; shift forecast 1–2 days ahead to reflect event-driven volatility.
- If sentiment is neutral or bearish and true outcome shows mean reversion (e.g., 3–5 days of decline followed by rebound), model often fails to anticipate reversal; add 1–2% upward bias for 3–5 days after mean reversion trigger.
- For long-term (30d) forecasts, if recent sentiment is mixed or bearish, model tends to overestimate recovery; reduce forecast mean by 2–4% if true outcome shows persistent decline.
